stories.title_en: A Woman Marries a Street-Sweeper and Costs Him His Life

paragraphs.en: In the capital lived a man named Fang Ba, dull-witted and earning his living by scavenging the streets. He had only an old mother at home. One day, while scavenging, he went to a small river to wash himself. Toward evening, a woman dressed in hemp mourning clothes stood nearby and waited until he finished washing. She then said to Fang Ba, "I am heading to my maiden family's home, but I cannot arrive tonight. May I rest at your house for the night?" Fang Ba replied, "My home is no place to stay. Why not go to an inn?" The woman said, "Inns are crowded with all sorts of people; lodging there is inconvenient. Who else lives in your house?" Fang Ba answered, "Only my old mother." The woman replied, "If you have a mother, then we can stay together."

Fang Ba led her home. The woman gave silver to buy rice, wine, and dishes, and at night the three ate together. She asked, "Has he taken a wife?" The mother said, "We can barely get through the day. Where would we get silver for a daughter-in-law?" The woman said, "My former husband is dead and already buried. I have no kin at home. I have gathered my household goods to go back to my mother's, but her house is far. I see your son is filial and kind. Meeting by chance seems Heaven's match. I would like to be your daughter-in-law and serve you morning and night. How would that be?" The mother said, "You mean well, but I fear my son cannot feed three mouths." The woman said, "I have also brought a little silver to start with. If I work diligently at needlework, it should be enough." Fang Ba was pleased: "My fortune this year says I should get a good wife. Each person has their own allotted lot. Why worry we cannot feed ourselves?" That night they became husband and wife and slept together. In one night they gave themselves over to every pleasure of love. The man said he had never married, and now it was like thirst meeting drink; the woman said she had long been without a mate, and now it was like heat meeting cool. They loved each other truly like fish in water. The mother too was overjoyed at Heaven's gift of a worthy daughter-in-law.

The next day, the woman gave her husband six qian of silver to buy rice and vegetables. On the third day, she asked her mother-in-law, "Why not have some clothes made?" The old woman said she had no silver. The woman then produced another six qian and told her husband to buy cloth at Merchant Wang’s large shop. Fang Ba, having already secured a wife and accumulated silver over time, was flushed with triumph. He went to Wang’s shop, bought two bolts of blue cloth, and returned home. The woman cut three feet from each bolt, then deliberately took a ruler and said, "This is leftover cut cloth, not a full bolt. How were we cheated? Take it back and exchange it. We paid good silver for cloth; how can they short us like this?" Fang Ba listened to his wife and went to exchange it. Wang’s shop retorted, "When did we ever have remnant cloth? You cut it yourself to cheat us." The two argued. Wang ordered his men to give them two more bolts. When he brought them home, the woman, behind his back, stabbed several folds with scissors, then spread them out and said again, "How is it you exchanged two more bolts of crushed, ruined cloth? This shop is hateful! They see you are simple, so they dare lie to you. If they won't exchange this time, curse them out loud. What is there to fear?" Stirred up by his wife, Fang Ba went in a rage and said, "You tricked us with broken cloth." Wang replied, "You buy one bolt and come to exchange it many times. What shop has time for that?" He refused to exchange. Fang Ba then let fly with filthy abuse. Wang grew angry, ordered his men to drag him and beat him, then opened the two bolts, inspected them, and threw them at him. Fang Ba took the cloth home and recounted the beating with resentment. The wife stamped her foot in anger: "We paid silver for cloth and instead got a beating. He relies on money and power. Fight him tooth and nail. Your mother and I can plead your wrong." She stirred her husband up again to go to the shop and cause a violent scene. Wang’s household men rose together and beat him badly; he came home with heavy wounds. The woman wept: "We must file a complaint to hold them liable for the wounds." She went to the censor and had the complaint accepted. Coming home, she bought good wine and dishes, and urged her husband to drink heavily so the bruising would disperse. Urged by her, he got dead drunk. That night, while he was drunk, she bound his hands and feet tight, stuffed sand in his mouth and nose, and by the third watch he had long been dead. She untied the ropes. Then she deliberately cried, "Your son’s body is cold and stiff—can he be dead?" The frightened mother rose to look: her son was dead. The two wept together in full mourning, then went back to the censor to file an additional complaint. Officers examined and impounded the body: there were heavy wounds all over. Wang the merchant was terrified and at a loss.

Three days before the hearing, the woman and her mother-in-law went to merchant Wang's cloth shop and said, "Your beating killed my husband—that is certain. My mother-in-law is old, and I alone cannot support us. Having you pay with your life helps no one. If you can provide three hundred taels to support my mother-in-law, she can withdraw the complaint and waive the inquest." Delighted at the offer, Wang sent an intermediary to negotiate and agreed to pay two hundred taels for Fang's mother's upkeep. Following the woman's instructions, the mother herself submitted a settlement statement: "I am poor and old; my son is dead, and my daughter-in-law is a widow. We have no means of survival. At the urging of relatives and neighbors, let Wang pay one hundred taels for my upkeep, and waive the inquest." The official approved the settlement, ordered Wang beaten with twenty strokes of the bamboo, imposed a heavy penalty, and allowed Fang Ba's wife to collect the silver and return home. Two days later, the woman stole the two hundred taels and fled under cover of night, vanishing without a trace. When Fang's mother sought to file another complaint, Wang paid another twenty taels to hush the matter up.

Note: This woman was the wife of a veteran con man. They had discovered that Fang Ba had only this old mother, so they sent the woman to pretend to be his wife, provoked him into a brawl with a rich shop, then beat him to death with added force. The mother would surely sue, and they would surely get silver; then they would make off with the silver and flee. Thus, they sacrificed a man's life to gain a fat profit. When the world's treachery has come to this, can anyone still be simple-hearted enough to walk into such traps?

stories.title_en: A Matchmaker Cons a Provincial Graduate into 'Marrying' a Titled Lady

paragraphs.en: Hong Zixuan, a Fujian provincial graduate, was in the capital preparing to take a concubine. Matchmakers led him to view several women, none of whom pleased him. There happened to be a titled lady of the Cui house, nearly thirty, yet still graceful as a maiden. Having completed her mourning period for her husband, she had gone to a temple to hold rites. Two sharpers had devised their scheme: one, posing as a matchmaker, first led Graduate Hong to the temple to see her himself. Hong found her appearance refined and her speech and bearing dignified, and was greatly delighted. The matchmaker said, "Since she suits you, we must speak to her elder brother-in-law; this woman’s marriage is arranged by him." He led the graduate straight to the house, first slipping fifty cash into his sleeve, went inside, and handed them to a young page: "A graduate has come to inspect your fine residence; please ask for three cups of tea for him." He then came out again and invited the graduate: "Her elder brother-in-law is out but will return shortly. Come sit in the hall." Shortly after, a trickster, posing as the elder brother, entered from outside. The three exchanged formalities, sat down again, and the young servant brought tea. The matchmaker said, "Your younger brother’s wife wishes to remarry. This Fujian graduate seeks to marry her and respectfully asks how much betrothal silver is required." The "elder brother" replied, "The road is rather far; I fear her natal family will not agree." The matchmaker said, "He will soon take office and can have her brother accompany him to the post; why fear the distance? Besides, he comes from an official family for generations, with in-laws filling the court; even in the capital many will look after her. This opportunity must not be missed. Only his lordship has not yet seen your younger brother’s wife." The elder brother smiled: "My younger brother’s wife is first among women in character and conduct, and in the past would not let people see her. Today her mourning is over; she is holding rites at such-and-such a temple. To go there and see her is easy." The matchmaker said, "From a house like yours, there is no need to see her. Just ask when she will leave and what the betrothal silver should be." The elder brother said, "Her mourning is over; she can leave anytime. The betrothal silver must be a hundred taels or more; her jewelry and trousseau are also worth fifty or sixty taels." He then led the matchmaker aside and whispered, "My congratulatory gift must be forty taels; do not let my brother’s wife know. The bride-price can be reduced a little." He sat down again and added, "If the silver is handed over tomorrow, do it in the garden lodge. There is a household superstition; we do not accept silver in the house." The matchmaker said, "It would be better to invite her brother to meet as well." The elder brother said, "If he comes, he will talk too much. After the marriage, it will not be too late to send word." He then saw the matchmaker and the graduate out. The matchmaker said, "Just now the elder brother told me the congratulatory silver must be forty taels, and the bride-price can be reduced a little. He does not want his brother’s wife to know, and wants the silver handed over in the garden."

The next day, the matchmaker led the graduate and two stewards to the garden lodge, then went to invite the Cui elder brother, who arrived with a young servant carrying a balance. The matchmaker said, "We should have someone write the betrothal letter." The elder brother asked, "My late brother isn't here—what use is a marriage letter?" The matchmaker replied, "Transactions in the capital differ from those in your home prefecture; even a simple account serves as proof." The elder brother offered, "Shall I write it myself?" "Best," said the matchmaker, and paper was produced. When they reached the section on betrothal silver, the elder brother said, "Sixty taels." "Reduce it," countered the matchmaker. "Just forty. Just ensure your brother's widow is well provided for; no need to demand much silver." The elder brother noted, "Both sums can be equal." "Easy enough," said the matchmaker. Once written, the matchmaker declared, "Keep the marriage letter in my hand while we weigh out the silver." First, they weighed forty taels into a single sealed packet, then weighed twenty taels and handed them to the elder brother. The elder brother rose: "I'll take the forty taels. The betrothal gift can be delivered at the house in her presence; otherwise, there's nothing to discuss." "Add another ten taels," insisted the matchmaker. The elder brother refused. The matchmaker turned to the graduate: "What do you say?" The graduate suggested, "Combine the forty taels in your hand, and deliver them to the woman at their house." The matchmaker countered, "Both the marriage letter and the silver must remain in my hand; we go together to the house and make the exchange." The elder brother argued, "This wasn't decided today; it was agreed yesterday that delivery would happen without her immediate presence. If the deal falls through, how could I keep it?" The matchmaker took only the forty taels and the marriage letter, returned to the inn with the graduate, and hired men to fetch the bride. He gave the marriage letter to the graduate, saying, "The matter is settled; no need to take it along." Then, taking only the two stewards and a dozen men, he went to the Cui house and sat by the side of the hall. "I'll call the elder brother," he said, before slipping away.

The Cui household saw so many people coming and asked, “What is your business?” The stewards said, “We have come to fetch a bride.” The Cui people said, “You have the wrong door. What bride?” The stewards said, “The matchmaker led us. How could we be wrong?” The Cui people said, “Which of you is the matchmaker?” The stewards said, “The matchmaker went to call your elder brother-in-law.” The Cui people said, “What elder brother-in-law?” The stewards said, “The one in your house who took the silver and gives the bride in marriage.” The Cui people spat in their faces: “You pack of lowborns, you deserve to die! This is Lord Cui’s residence. Who fooled you into talking this nonsense here?” The stewards said, “Yesterday we drank tea in your house with Master Hong, agreed on a marriage, already handed over silver in the garden, and now you go back on it. Are we afraid of you? Think you can make off with our silver?” The Cui people said, “Who gave you tea, who took your silver? Who in our house is to be married out?” The stewards said, “The lady who was having rites in the temple the other day wants to remarry.” The Cui people said, “Pah! That is our mistress, who holds an imperial patent of rank. Who can marry her! We will report to the patrol officer and have this pack of swindlers locked up!” The two stewards, seeing the matchmaker did not come back with the “elder brother,” grew uneasy and each fled to the inn. The Cui people followed, found it was Graduate Hong Zixuan forcing a marriage, and went to the prefect to charge him with forcibly marrying a titled lady. When Hong heard of the charge he knew he had been swindled, and fled the capital. When the prefect sent men to bring him in, they reported he had already gone, vanished with no known destination. The prefect said, “Of course he would run. How would he dare face it!” So the case was filed for the record, to be taken up later.

Note: The swindlers' cleverness lay in seeing that Lady Cui and her servants were all at the temple; they then tricked a junior household servant into serving tea. They also claimed the brother-in-law wished to avoid being seen openly asking for celebratory gifts and wanted the silver handed over in the garden lodge—thus enabling the fraud. Graduate Hong lost his silver and was forced to flee on top of it. Moreover, the prefect believed the story of an attempted abduction and opened an official case. Taking a concubine away from home and expecting things to go smoothly? Truly difficult! How can one ever act without verifying the facts?

stories.title_en: Taking a Concubine in Another Province Triggers a Lawsuit Disaster

paragraphs.en: Cai Tianshou of Guangdong was open-handed and stood by his word. At forty he had no son, and his wife was such a shrew that she would not let him take a concubine. One day he brought more than thirty loads of Guangdong tin to Suzhou to sell, and said to the broker Xiao Hanqing, "I still have no son, and I would like to take a concubine here. Is there anyone suitable on reasonable terms?" Hanqing said, "When you have silver, why worry about finding a girl to your liking?" He led him to look at several unmarried girls, but none suited: "I am past forty; these girls are too young to be a match for my years, so I will not take them."

There happened to be a wastrel named Guo Yanji. His household included a widowed mother, née Deng, thirty-three years old, of decent looks. When her husband died, he left a thousand taels; Yanji gambled it all away and still owed over twenty taels in gambling debts, pressing him with no way to pay. He plotted with a crook to pretend his mother was his wife, intending to marry her off to settle the debt. Word reached Hanqing through a matchmaker. He took Tianshou to inspect her; age and appearance suited them, and they agreed on a bride-price of a little over forty taels. Yanji said, "She comes from across the river. I fear her natal family will block it and not let her marry far. Seal the silver with the broker. When you are about to board, I will have her sent to the boat, and person and silver can be exchanged." The broker thought this would do.

When it was time to depart, Yanji hired a sedan chair himself and fabricated a story that his maternal uncle's house was sending for his mother. After boarding the boat, she learned only then that her son had sold her off in marriage to a traveling merchant. Deeply enraged, she held her temper and asked, "Since you have married me off to someone, why hide it from me? And who is the man marrying me?" Tianshou replied, "It is this unworthy one." The woman said, "Seeing you, I take you for a man of means, so I harbor no grudge. But because my late husband squandered everything in gambling, I hid all my clothes and jewelry at my mother's home. Let me take you there to fetch them, and at the same time let my family know." Tianshou believed her and went along with Mistress Deng. Once inside, she poured out the tale of how her son had secretly married her off behind her back. Her elder brother Deng Tianming flared up in fury: "Where has anyone ever heard of a son daring to marry off his own mother! And what traveler has the insolence to take her?" He rushed out and began beating Tianshou wildly. Mistress Deng stepped in to stop him: "The traveler surely knew nothing of the scheme; only that unfilial Yanji has the brazen nerve that deserves death!" Tianming immediately drew up a complaint and filed it with the county. Magistrate Zou accepted the suit and dispatched runners to arrest Yanji, who went into hiding and could not be found; so they first brought in Hanqing and Tianshou. When Magistrate Zou learned the facts, he was furious. He had the marriage contractor and the matchmaker each given twenty strokes, remanded Tianshou to jail, and ordered Hanqing to produce Yanji. Months passed, yet Yanji still could not be captured, and Hanqing was repeatedly hauled in under deadlines and beaten. Tianshou sought to pull strings through influential backers to secure his release, but Magistrate Zou flatly refused. Someone advised Tianshou: "A thief takes a thief to catch; a gambler takes a gambler to catch. Why not promise a silver reward to gamblers to capture him?" Within a few days, local rogues pointed out Yanji's hiding place, and the runners arrested him. Magistrate Zou tried the case and established that Yanji, as a son, had married his own mother off to a distant traveler as a concubine. He sentenced him to forty strokes of the heavy cane and recommended the severest statutory punishment, confiscating the purchase money to the public coffers. Hanqing and Tianshou were each sentenced to caning as punishment. As for the mother, Mistress Deng, she was handed over to her brother Deng Tianming to care for at home, leaving her free to choose her own remarriage if she wished, and official clearance was granted.

Note: Taking a concubine for the sake of an heir is not forbidden by ritual or law. Only, one should take her from a nearby small household. If you go to another province and marry out of lust for looks, you often brew later trouble. Cases of this kind may serve as a stark warning.

stories.title_en: A Frog Exposes a Murderous Marriage Plot

paragraphs.en: Chen Cai of Xuzhou was enormously rich, deep and close in his schemes, possessing the cunning of Wang Mang and Cao Cao. At thirty, neither his wife nor concubines had borne him a son. A neighbor named Pan often borrowed silver from Cai to go out trading. While visiting the Pan household, Chen saw that Pan’s wife, surnamed You, was unmatched in beauty, and an evil thought arose in him. He invited Pan to invest together, buying cotton at Guazhou to sell in Guangzhou and elsewhere. Once the goods were sold, they traveled home together. Their route passed the West Gate ferry, a secluded spot with little traffic. Upon boarding, a pole was used to push the boat. Chen secretly thought, "This chance can be seized." From behind, he shoved Pan into the river. When Pan broke the surface, Chen again used the pole to push him down into the depths. After Pan drowned, Chen deliberately summoned fishermen to retrieve the body, had it burned, wrapped the bones, and headed home.

Dressed in white mourning clothes, Cai went to see Pan's parents, wept loudly first, and then reported the tragic news. The entire household wailed and asked in detail how he had died. Cai said, "While crossing at the West Gate ferry, he boarded the boat and took the pole to push off, and plunged into the water along with the pole. The water was deep and swift, and he lacked the strength to come back up, so he drowned. I hired men to recover his body, cremated his bones, and brought them home." When he finished speaking, the Pan household wept again. Cai then accounted clearly for the sales ledger and all the capital, item by item, and returned them to the parents. The whole family felt grateful for his kindness—how could they know that Cai himself had plotted the murder?

Half a year later, Pan Yu, now old and unable to support his two young grandsons, proposed taking a man into the family as a live-in son-in-law to manage the household, and discussed this with Cai. Cai replied, "A live-in marriage is a long-term affair; one must secure the right man. Otherwise, the house will be ruined, and regret will come too late. In my humble opinion, it is best to carefully maintain the household and uphold widowhood rather than remarrying." Cai spoke thus, but his true design ran much deeper. Whenever anyone was proposed as a live-in son-in-law, Yu would consult Cai, who always found a way to thwart the match. First, however, he bribed You Shi’s natal family.

When the plot was set, he said to Yu, "I am very close to your son; there is no reason I should move in myself. But sometimes one must weigh principle against expediency. Try discussing this with your uncle." Yu asked, "What is your view?" Cai replied, "I propose that you hand over all your property to me to manage. Please have your clan relatives draw up a document specifying how much each year will supply you and your wife for food and daily needs, how much for ancestral graves and labor service, and the rest kept for you to provide for the two grandsons' marriages. Let your daughter-in-law become my secondary wife. My own humble wife is virtuous; there will surely be no jealousy. Later, if we have children, I will not neglect her. Thus, your daughter-in-law will have a secure place, and the family will have someone to rely on." The daughter-in-law said, "It is said, 'Better to be a poor man's wife than a rich man's concubine.' My husband was his friend; if I marry him as a concubine, it will look bad. Please, Father-in-law, consider again." Yu said, "It is rare to find a household so wealthy and honest, and he will manage our affairs besides. I can sit back and enjoy food and clothing without labor; the remainder is saved for the grandsons' marriages. The agreement is witnessed by my clansmen. How secure that is! No need to doubt further." The entire Pan household agreed; You Shi's parents also unanimously said, "Agreed." You Shi had no choice but to obey.

Unawares, over twenty years had passed since the marriage; she had borne two sons and raised an eldest grandson. Both older sons had married and also produced two grandsons. Cai's principal wife had died ten years prior, yet You Shi and her husband lived in perfect harmony. One day, rain poured down until the courtyard flooded. Suddenly, a frog soaked in the water leaped onto the hall. Cai used a small bamboo stick to poke it back into the water, repeating this several times. Ordinarily a man of few words, that day Heaven revealed his inner thoughts. He thought: "You Shi has been affectionate for so long; if I mention the past, she surely won't resent me." Unintentionally, he let slip: 'Your former husband was just like this frog. If I hadn't hatched a scheme, how could I have become your husband?' You Shi asked, "What scheme?" Cai replied, "Back then, seeing your unmatched beauty, I wanted you in my bed. I devised a plan under the guise of trade. At the river crossing, I kicked him into the waves. Your husband broke the surface, so I used my pole to push him back into the deep abyss. Twice or thrice he rose, and I pushed him down—just like this frog." You Shi cried out in shock and cursed loudly: "You wolf-hearted thief! You deserve a thousand cuts! Who is so vicious!" Cursed by his wife, Cai had no answer. You Shi ran weeping into the road, shouting, "This thief murdered my former husband and plotted to make me his concubine! I will go to the officials to avenge my husband!" Neighbors on both sides heard and were shocked. Cai ordered his two sons to forcibly drag You Shi inside; they all knelt and pleaded, "Think of the honor of our entire household; do not say such things." You Shi pointed and cursed her sons: 'Your father's treacherous plot—how can sons flourish? He did evil without cause, far too violent. He harmed his trading partner with dark, crooked treachery; Heaven revealed his heart, and he boasted of it himself. I will take it to the officials to clear this wicked crime, cut off his head to restore moral order. Though my husband has returned to yellow earth, under the Nine Springs his heart will find peace.'

The eldest son, Pan Huai, and the second, Pan Yang, heard their mother You going about spreading news that Chen Cai had murdered their father, and came with the Pan clan to ask for details. You Shi, seeing her two sons and her husband’s younger brother, wept bitterly and said: “When your father was alive and went out trading, he often borrowed capital from this thief. He saw that I was handsome then, and an evil thought arose. He invited your father out to trade; returning at the West Gate ferry, he kicked your father into the river. When he broke the surface, he used the pole again to push him down into the deep. Several times like this, and so he drowned.” They asked, “How do you know?” You Shi said: “Just now in the heavy rain the courtyard overflowed. A frog was soaked and leaped onto the hall. The thief beat it with bamboo and poked it down several times; the frog, worn out by the beating, drowned. Heaven will not tolerate treachery. He saw this frog and confessed his own guilt; that is how I know. You sons can go and charge him; I will come as witness.” Huai and Yang heard this, beat their breasts, cried to heaven, and wept: “This feud cannot share the same sky. Drag him here and beat him to death!” They went straight into the inner hall, seized Chen Cai, and beat him. Cai’s household, being in the wrong, naturally dared not fight back. Cai said in anger: “Even if I plotted against a man, the law has a clear article. How dare you beat me?” You Shi said: “His crime is so great that death is insufficient. If we have not gone through the officials and kill him by a wrong blow, then the feud is not avenged and we have made a homicide case instead.” In the midst of the uproar, more than a hundred of the Pan clan gathered; among them some ne’er-do-wells wanted to loot the house. You Shi said: “The goods are mine. The thief has broken the law and should die; they are not his. If I do not come forward to prove his crime, how may you lot plunder my property?”

You Shi and her two sons clutched the petition and rushed to the county magistrate to report the crime. Magistrate Wei accepted their complaint, ordered Chen Cai brought to court. Without a word of denial, he confessed to everything. Magistrate Wei beat Cai thirty strokes, immediately sentenced him to death, and reported the case to the superior authorities. You Shi and her two sons, Huai and Yang, each posted bail to await transfer to the provincial courts. That day, hundreds gathered at the county office to watch. They all said: "This woman was originally in the Pan household, living in a respectable station; now she is with Chen, a man worth ten thousand taels of gold, commanding slaves and maids, first a concubine and now the principal wife. Years have passed, and she has borne sons and grandsons. A sentimental person, upon first hearing of this, would likely choke up, swallow their voice, and let it drop. But she went straight to the public court, demanding the life for her former husband. She can truly be called a woman of honor among her sex, acting beyond the common run!"

The two courts had finished reviewing the case; Chen Cai’s capital sentence was fixed. Cai asked a jailer to summon You Shi and their two sons to the prison to give his final instructions. You Shi refused to go see him; she only sent her two sons. Cai charged them to pass word: “I am to pay Pan’s life; that is settled. Her grievance is paid, and the debt of that old wrong has been repaid. Why begrudge seeing me once? I have final arrangements I wish to entrust.” You Shi said, “All kindness and duty between us are cut. What face do I have to see him again?” The two sons went into the jail and answered. Cai said in a great rage, “I suffer every misery in jail and will be executed any day. She enjoys wealth at home—is it the Pan house’s goods, or the Chen house’s?” When he had finished, the two sons passed their father’s words to their mother. You Shi said, “I was in your father’s house for over twenty years; the kindness was not shallow. I only did not know how clever his schemes were. Now that the past has come out, your father is in truth my enemy, and by right I must cut him off. You two are of my flesh and blood; how could I bear to give you up? Your father need not say the wealth is his house’s; I already meant to go back to the Pan house. Now that he has spoken so, my mind to return is fixed. Take your mother as already dead; think of me no more.” The two sons said, “Mother avenging her former husband is exactly great duty; our father has no call to resent it. Only think that we brothers are young and still depend on Mother’s teaching. By all means do not go to that other house.” You Shi would not listen. She gathered the Chen clan, handed over the estate, jewelry, and everything else clearly, and went back empty-handed to the Pan house, content to live simply. People all admired her high sense of duty, envied Pan for having such a wife, so that the feud was at last repaid, and sighed that Cai’s treacherous plot had brought the disaster back on himself.
